title: Retry guardrails and hedged-request patterns library
creator: Asha Patel
description: Create a language-agnostic, well-tested library and runtime contract for retry/timeout/backoff and hedged requests across Redwood services and SDKs. The goal is to provide guardrails that preserve SLOs, enable safe multi-region failover, and integrate with circuit breakers and load-shedding policies. This ticket drives the spec, prototype libraries (Go + Python + TS), runtime hooks, and a canary rollout plan for internal services and the public SDKs.
acceptance_criteria: Spec document (RFC) approved by SRE/Product/SDK leads describing: idempotency key semantics, hedging shape, timeout/deadline hierarchy, and load-shedding primitives
Reference implementation libraries available for Go, Python, and TypeScript with consistent public APIs
SDKs expose optional hedging API and idempotency key parameter; default behavior is safe for non-idempotent endpoints
Runtime integration added to serving runtime to honor hedged requests and emit observability metrics (hedge_attempts, hedge_latency, hedge_outcome)
Feature flags and rollout plan defined; canary traffic to 3 internal services without SLO regressions
E2E tests that simulate multi-region outage and validate correct failover behavior without duplicate side-effects when idempotency keys present
Documentation and examples for application developers and platform engineers
decisions: Adopt a dual-mode hedging model: optimistic client-side hedging with server-side acknowledgment to avoid duplicate processing
Idempotency keys will be opaque strings scoped by API and tenant; servers must validate deterministically and store outcome references for 24h by default
Backoff defaults: jittered exponential starting at 50ms, multiplier 2, max backoff 2s for interactive RPCs; longer for async batch endpoints (configurable per route)
Timeout hierarchy: caller deadline > SDK retry loop deadline > per-attempt hard timeout. SDK will honor explicit deadlines passed from callers
Circuit breaker integration: hedged requests count against circuit breaker budget; runtime allows preference for single attempt when breaker open and traffic is critical
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (spec + prototype): Draft RFC and implement minimal Go client library + runtime hooks to emit hedge metrics (2 weeks)
Phase 2 (SDKs): Implement Python and TypeScript clients, align public API shapes, add integration tests (3 weeks)
Phase 3 (runtime + server): Wire server-side hedging acknowledgements, idempotency outcome store, and make hedging opt-in per route (3 weeks)
Phase 4 (integrations): Add circuit-breaker and load-shed adapters, instrumentation, and dashboards (2 weeks)
Phase 5 (rollout): Canary to internal services, iterate on defaults, then public SDK release (2 weeks)
rollout_plan: Create feature flag hedging.v1 default=false; enable for internal services Svc-A, Svc-B, Svc-C at 5% traffic
Monitor hedging metrics and SLOs for 48h; roll back if error rate or latency regressions exceed thresholds
Gradually increase to 25% then 100% for internal services; during each step validate idempotency-store hit-rate and duplicate-side-effects count
Open SDK beta to selected customers with opt-in flag and support channel guidance
After 6 weeks of stable signals, flip default to enabled for interactive endpoints and publish migration guide
testing_plan: Unit tests for client libraries covering retry/backoff, deadline propagation, and hedging decisions
Integration test harness that simulates slow/failed regions and validates only-one-side-effect when idempotency key present
Chaos tests: kill primary region replicas and verify client hedging + multi-region failover maintains SLOs
Load tests to ensure hedged fanout does not cause runtime overload; validate load-shedding tokens and circuit-breaker throttling
Fuzz testing for malformed idempotency keys and header strip/forwarding correctness
open_questions: What is the persistence window for idempotency outcome records in high-cardinality tenants? (cost vs safety tradeoff)
Should hedging be on by default for all interactive endpoints or only for routes the runtime marks as hedging-safe?
How do we expose hedging observability to customers without leaking internal topology details?
Do we provide an escape hatch for SDK users to force single-attempt behavior for cost-sensitive workloads?
